name: Anita Nose Adjuster

lead: The Anita nose adjuster belongs to a family of mechanical nose shapers sold from the nineteenth century into the 1920s and after. They were small clamps, plates or shells fitted over the nose, tightened with screws or straps, and marketed as a painless, inexpensive way to straighten or reshape the nose at home.

For a looks-minded user the appeal was a different nose profile without an operation. Makers of comparable devices said the cartilage was soft enough to be moulded with regular wear. No clinical trial of such devices is known, and a modern account of trying one reports that it did not produce lasting change.

paras: Devices of this type were worn for an hour a day or overnight, fitted around the nose with adjustable screws or plates and held on with a band. Vendors advised wearing them for weeks or months.

Reported problems with comparable shapers include disturbed sleep and cuts or marks from sharp metal parts. Pressure on the nose and surrounding skin is a general concern for any tight device worn for long periods.

lead: The Anita nose adjuster is a vintage mechanical device of the nose-shaper type: an appliance fitted over the nose and tightened to press it toward a different shape. Such devices were sold as discreet, low-cost alternatives to surgery for people unhappy with the profile of their nose.

The category has a documented history. In London, perfumer Alexander Ross advertised a boxwood nose machine from 1871, and the German Zello-Punkt, a brass nose shaper patented in 1894, was sold through hairdressers and pharmacies [1][2]. Appearance communities and collectors now discuss these gadgets as period curiosities.

paras: Nose shapers varied in construction. Alexander Ross's nose machine, introduced in late 1871 in London, was a small wooden clamp of two curved boxwood pieces held by two screws, sold for 10s 6d [2]. The Zello-Punkt, patented in 1894 by Professor G. von Eck, was a moulded brass shell shaped like a nose, with adjusting screws, a front plate, thin leather-cushioned inner plates and an elastic band around the head [1].

Makers presented the devices as painless and cheap compared with operations. The Ross advertisement said wearing the machine for an hour a day would let the soft cartilage take on the desired shape, and the Zello-Punkt was sold in hairdressers' shops and pharmacies with instructions to wear it for several months and to soften the skin with wax beforehand [1][2]. Newspapers of the period treated the nose machine as a novelty [2].

A modern writer who tried a Zello-Punkt doubted it could produce lasting results, noting that any effect depended on band tension and that pressure on the tissue lasted only minutes, and reported disturbed sleep and facial injuries from the sharp metal [1].
